notes:
# Nehemiah 10: verse-by-verse research notes

**Gaps in what I found:** I didn't find any netbible.org notes, Lutheran or Pentecostal sources specific to this chapter, Orthodox material, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace treatment of these verses. Where commentaries are labelled by tradition below, the labels come from StudyLight's own tags.

---

## vv. 1–27: Those who sealed the covenant

**v. 1**
- This chapter follows on from Nehemiah 9:38. Guzik says the Hebrew phrase there is literally "cut" a covenant, because covenants were usually made with an animal sacrifice. The nation as a whole now does something about its decision by entering a covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/
- Guzik also counts the leaders (84 in all) willing to put their names on the line for the covenant before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says Nehemiah's name comes first because of his high official rank, as deputy of the Persian monarch. It adds that the people were represented by their elders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-1.htm
- On Zedekiah, Ellicott thinks he is probably Zadok the scribe (Nehemiah 13:13), Nehemiah's secretary. The Cambridge Bible instead suggests a Persian official ranking next to Nehemiah, or one of royal line (e.g. of the house of Zerubbabel). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-1.htm
- **Why isn't Ezra named?** Benson guesses he was prevented by some sickness, or other extraordinary impediment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-1.htm The Expositor's Bible suggests instead that only heads of houses affixed their seals, and that Ezra was not accounted one of them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/nehemiah/10.htm
- The Expositor's Bible also takes Nehemiah heading the list as a sign that as yet even in a religious document the civil ruler takes precedence of the hierarchy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/nehemiah/10.htm

**vv. 2–8 (the priests)**
- Barnes says the names are not personal, but designate families. He thinks the seal of the high-priestly house of Seraiah was probably appended either by Ezra or Eliashib. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-10.htm
- The Expositor's Bible notes that most of these names reappear in the list in Nehemiah 12:1–7. It also flags a most significant omission: the high priest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/nehemiah/10.htm
- Gill says some think the high priest Eliashib had not behaved well in his office. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-10.htm
- Coffman explains why the priests come before the Levites here, the reverse of chapter 9. In chapter 9 the Levites led the prayer, but at the signing the priests, who ranked higher than the Levites, naturally had preference in the order of their signing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/nehemiah-10.html
- Precept Austin cross-references each name to other places it appears in Nehemiah, mostly chapters 3, 11 and 12. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary

**vv. 9–13 (the Levites)**
- Gill counts the Levites in all seventeen, most of which we have met with in this book before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-10.htm
- Precept Austin links Jeshua, Shebaniah, Sherebiah and others to the Levites who led the Law-reading and prayer in chapters 8 and 9. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary

**vv. 14–27 (the leaders of the people)**
- Ellicott: some of the names are personal, some belong to families, some represent places. Compared with Ezra 2, years had added to the number of the houses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/nehemiah-10.html
- Gill counts 44 leaders, and 84 sealers in all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-10.htm
- The Catholic commentator Haydock notes that many of these names appear as returning from Babylon in chapter 7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/nehemiah/10.htm

---

## vv. 28–29: The whole people join the oath

**v. 28**
- Ellicott asks whether "all who had separated themselves" means converts from paganism. He doubts it, because there is no record as yet of a recognised body of such proselytes. He says "able to understand" means children who could intelligently take the oath were included. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/nehemiah-10.html
- Haydock and Pett, by contrast, take the "separated" to include converts (proselytes). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/nehemiah/10.htm, https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-10.html
- Guzik says the oath was made in public because a public covenant meant accountability. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/

**v. 29**
- Ellicott: the oath assumed the obligation; the curse imprecated the penalty of violation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-29.htm
- Benson notes the nobles are called "brothers," for in the things of God, rich and poor, high and low, meet together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-29.htm
- Bob Utley calls this a covenant renewal service, built on the blessings and curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary
- Guzik applies the "curse" to believers today. Praying "Lord, whatever it takes" is essentially praying the same thing, and that is a good prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/
- **Should Christians make formal covenants like this?** Sources differ:
  - The Expositor's Bible takes a cautious view. It says a formal pledge is scarcely in accordance with the spirit of the gospel, and prefers turning our vows into prayers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/nehemiah/10.htm
  - The Biblical Illustrator (W. Ritchie), by contrast, draws from the chapter the propriety of religious covenanting. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/10-32.html

---

## vv. 30–31: Specific promises

**v. 30 (marriage)**
- Utley says this does not refer to racial exclusion, but religious exclusion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary
- Henry Morris notes the problem had already caused trouble in Ezra 9–10 and came back again in Nehemiah 13:23–25. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary
- Guzik points out that the promise was addressed to parents, who arranged marriages then. He applies the principle today: believers should marry believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/

**v. 31 (Sabbath, holy days, the seventh year)**
- Benson says they would not even buy food on the sabbath, but would buy their supplies the day before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-31.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Nehemiah later enforced stricter rules (13:15–22). It also notes that leaving the land unfarmed every seventh year had been neglected before the exile, and that this neglect was one of the sins the exile punished (2 Chronicles 36:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-31.htm
- The Geneva Study Bible notes the people broke soon after this promise (Neh. 13:15). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-31.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) concludes that trading on holy days is therefore sinful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/nehemiah/10.htm
- **Debts: cancelled or paused?** Sources disagree.
  - Utley says all debts were cancelled on the seventh year. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-10
  - The Cambridge Bible calls that a common error. Like fallow land, it says, the debts stayed but were not collected for a year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-31.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible reads this verse as drawing on several law codes in the Pentateuch, both "Priestly" and "Deuteronomic." It argues that Ezra's Law contained substantially all the component parts of our Pentateuch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-31.htm
- Guzik applies the verse to business ethics today: we should trust God rather than cut corners. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/

---

## vv. 32–39: Supporting God's house

**v. 32 (the third of a shekel)**
- Most older commentators say the Law's half-shekel was cut to a third in consequence of the general poverty of the people (JFB). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/nehemiah/10.htm
- Barnes and Ellicott see it differently: the law's half-shekel was only an occasional census tax, and this is the first annual temple tax, raised from the third of a shekel to half a shekel in later times (Matthew 17:24). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-32.htm
- Constable lists three possibilities: the amount was reduced because of poverty, it was paid on top of the half-shekel, or the shekel's value had changed. He concludes the text is not specific on this point. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/10-32.html
- **Modern scholarship:** The Cambridge Bible notes that some scholars think the half-shekel rule in Exodus 30 was added after Nehemiah's time. It also cites a coin study: a third of the Babylonian shekel was the same as the half of the ancient light shekel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-32.htm
- Coffman (labelled Arminian) argues that Jesus paying this tax showed he endorsed and approved the ordinance mentioned here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/10-32.html
- Pett calls the tax an act of benevolence and gratitude from a poor people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-10.html

**v. 33 (what the tax paid for)**
- Benson spells it out: the showbread, two lambs daily, four on Sabbaths, festival sacrifices and sin offerings, the charge of which was great and constant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/10-32.htm
- Utley notes that before the exile the king had paid these costs, but after the return they were shared among the people. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-10
- Haydock adds that the Persian kings' grants had been recalled, or were not well executed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/nehemiah/10.htm

**v. 34 (the wood offering)**
- Haydock (Catholic) says the people brought the wood, the Levites carried it into the temple and the priests laid it on the altar, all decided by lot. He says a festival called Xylophoria, was instituted about the month of August, citing Josephus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/nehemiah/10.htm
- The Expositor's Bible says the religion's survival centred on the altar fire, and its completion was attained in the supreme sacrifice of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/nehemiah/10.htm
- Guzik counts the wood and the tax as giving "as special need required." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/

**v. 35 (firstfruits)**
- Ellicott: the detailed listing implies that neglect had crept in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/nehemiah-10.html
- Guzik: giving the firstfruits took faith, since their land might not produce more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/

**v. 36 (firstborn)**
- Ellicott distinguishes "our livestock" (unclean animals) from "the firstlings of our herds and of our flocks." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/nehemiah-10.html

**v. 37 (tithes to the Levites)**
- The Believer's Study Bible says the firstfruits had been neglected, so that the Levites were not receiving needed support (compare Malachi 3:8). https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary
- Keil & Delitzsch discuss how to translate the end of the verse. They prefer the reading that the tithes are due to the Levites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/10-38.html

**v. 38 (the priest and the "tithe of the tithes")**
- JFB calls the priest going along a prudential arrangement, meant to stop the people cheating the Levites, or the Levites cheating the priests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/nehemiah/10.htm
- Utley calls it one of the checks and balances procedures. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary
- Coffman doesn't recall this rule from the Pentateuch and says it was there to prevent the Levite from cheating. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/10-38.html
- JFB: the Levites gave a tenth of what they received to the priests, and carried it to the temple stores. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/nehemiah-10.html

**v. 39 ("We will not neglect the house of our God")**
- Ellicott: the priests themselves were exempted from the care of gathering the tithes. He links both the promise and its later breaking to Nehemiah 13:11–14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/nehemiah-10.html
- Constable: this sentence shows the people's main concern was the worship that was the heart of their national life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/10-38.html
- Matthew Henry: we must not only cease to do evil, but learn to do well. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-10-commentary
- Guzik: they promised to *spend* money in ways that honour God, beginning it all with giving to the LORD. He adds that we cannot out-give God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-10/

---

## Where Protestant teachers really differ: must Christians tithe? (vv. 35–39)

- **For a binding tithe:** William Barcley (TGC) says the tithe is essential for holiness, vital for the ongoing work of Christ's church, and required for receiving God's blessing. He calls 10% a minimum. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/bible-commands-christians-to-tithe/
- **Against:** Tom Schreiner (TGC) says believers aren't under the Mosaic covenant. He adds that there are no Levites and priests in the new covenant, and that the tithe was tied to the land. He still urges generous giving, often more than 10%. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/7-reasons-christians-not-required-to-tithe/
- **Others against:** Bible.org argues tithing was a tax on the nation of Israel, and the full Old Testament total was nearer 22%. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-4-why-you-should-not-tithe-selected-scriptures GotQuestions holds that Christians are not obligated to give a 10-percent tithe, though some treat it as a recommended minimum. https://www.gotquestions.org/tithing-Christian.html
- **A broader caution:** The Expositor's Bible (older British Protestant) describes this covenant as a willing "bondage" to law, and rejoices in Christian freedom from its irksome restraints. It adds that the Christian is not an antinomian (that is, not free of all obligation). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/nehemiah/10.htm

These sources don't identify their authors' denominations, so I haven't tied any view to a particular church tradition.
